title: Shuttleboard routing constraints — weekly brief
content:
Context:
This is the midweek briefing from the Shuttleboard routing experiment group — focused on how routing constraints interact with KV cache pressure and microbatch hygiene. Goal: identify low-risk routing changes we can flip for the weekend canary without regressing p99 latency or increasing KV eviction churn.

Attendees (standup): Avery (owner), Ravi (kernel), Leah (kv/batching), Marta (SRE), Jon (bench).

Summary of what we measured (Apr 08–11 window):
- Short experiment A (route leash tightened for small requests): 6h run on canary cluster (s-rt-04). Results: p50 unchanged, p95 +4ms, p99 +18ms (baseline p99 = 102ms -> 120ms). Token throughput unchanged.
- Shadow drains enabled on warm nodes (prefill suppression): 12h run: KV cache hit-rate improved from 71% -> 76% on targeted cohorts, but eviction spikes at hour 6 correlated with long-running large sequence requests.
- Microbatch split test: splitting large microbatches (>32 requests) into two subbatches reduced jitter for small tails but increased overall GPU kernel invocations by ~9%, increasing cost-per-token by ~2.1%.

Observations and interpretation:
- Tightening the route leash (short-circuit routing) helps cost predictability but exposes kernels to slightly higher tail latencies because tiny requests lose batching opportunity. The p99 increase in Experiment A is primarily for short sequences under 64 tokens.
- The shadow drain idea meaningfully improves hot-key locality for KV-backed cohorts, but when a handful of long dialogs appear they 'contaminate' the cache and trigger synchronous prefetch cascades that ripple into eviction storms. This suggests we need a suppression rule for long sequences or a leak valve that prevents synchronous prefetch for cohorts flagged as high-variance.
- Microbatch splitting handles jitter but at GPU efficiency cost. The 9% kernel invocation delta aligns with our hypothesis around fragmentation overhead; this is acceptable for bursty tails but not for steady-state throughput-driven workloads.

Action items (owner -> due):
- Avery: draft a canary rollout plan that applies route leash only to cohorts with median seq_len <= 48. Target: roll to 5% on Friday 2029-04-12 03:00 UTC. (due 2029-04-12 10:00)
- Leah: implement a cohort-tagging filter in the prefill controller to mark high-variance cohorts (heuristic: 95th/median > 6) and bypass shadow-drain prefetch for them. (due 2029-04-15)
- Ravi: add telemetry to kernel scheduler to emit microbatch fragmentation count + per-kernel-invocation duration. Start with s-rt-*. (due 2029-04-13)
- Marta: prepare rollback playbook (node drain, model-fallback) and a runbook snippet for oncall to revert route leash. (due 2029-04-12 18:00)
- Jon: reproduce microbatch split cost numbers on bench cluster with 8xA800s and provide a flamegraph capture. (due 2029-04-14)

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- Is the p99 uplift in Experiment A purely due to loss of batching, or does route-change also change kernel path selection (we saw a slight uptick in fallback kernel in traces)?
- Can we design a lightweight prefill "leash" that only prefetches first N KV segments per request for cohorts with spike-prone sequences?
- Does cohort-level tagging introduce too much operational complexity for SRE during incidents? Need to prototype quick toggles.

Notes-to-self / quick debugging snippets:
- When reproducing the eviction spike, check dev trace id: trace:shuttle-evict-2029-04-09-21 (example in bench logs).
- To simulate a high-variance cohort: run bench load with 95% sequences random(8..32) and 5% sequences at 2048 tokens; observe cache churn after ~45min.

Decision log (temporary):
- Do not flip route leash to global canary yet. We accept a staged cohort-targeted canary for Friday.
- Shadow-drain remains enabled for low-variance cohorts; will add bypass for high-variance as an interim measure.

Follow-ups for next week:
- Short doc describing cohort tagging heuristics and how to toggle during incident response (Leah + Marta).
- Kernel scheduler telemetry landed and 48h run to observe fragmentation metrics (Ravi).
- Cost/latency tradeoff analysis of microbatch split vs. adaptive bundling (Jon + Avery).

Misc / loose ends:
- We spotted a weird trace where a 12-token request hit the large-sequence prefetch branch; likely a stale header causing misclassification. Need a sanity check in the classifier.
- Concurrency limiter threshold for the prefill controller currently set at 128; lowering to 96 reduced simultaneous prefetches by ~14% in a quick test but increased enqueue waits. More systematic sweep planned.

Appendix: quick metrics snapshot (canary cluster, 2029-04-11 23:00 UTC)
- p50: 22ms (baseline 22ms)
- p95: 68ms (baseline 64ms)
- p99: 120ms (baseline 102ms)
- KV hit-rate (cohort set X): 76% (baseline 71%)
- Kernel invocations per 1M tokens: 893 -> 974 (microbatch split experiment)

If anything is unclear or you want the raw bench traces, ping me on Slack (#serving-runtime) or drop a note in INF-6238.

— Avery
